name: Cologne Cathedral
label: Cologne Cathedral
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-16).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/4532022: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Cologne Cathedral' (170 m across).
notes: The twin-spired Gothic west facade seen from Kardinal-Höffner-Platz.

text.description: Cologne Cathedral (the Kölner Dom) is the great Gothic church that dominates the city, and it is easy to see why it is the first spot on this map. Its two spires reach 157 m, which makes it the tallest twin-spired church in the world. Together they give it the largest façade of any church. Building began in 1248 and stopped around 1560. Work started up again in the 1800s, and the cathedral was finished to its original medieval plan in 1880. It became a World Heritage Site in 1996 and is Germany's most visited landmark, so expect company. It was built to house the Shrine of the Three Kings, a medieval goldsmith's masterpiece. The cathedral photographs well because of its sheer scale and the dark, finely carved stonework, which gives your picture texture even in flat light. The challenge is fitting it all in. Stand back, keep your phone upright and level, and let the two towers frame the shot. Then step closer for details such as pinnacles, carvings and the doorways. Check the official site before you go if you plan to go inside or visit anything beyond the outside.
text.geographic_location: The cathedral stands in Cologne, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany. It is a large landmark, with an outline about 170 m across.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from the centre of Cologne and head for the cathedral. From there it is about 3 minutes on foot east to the building itself. The phone icon on the map is about 90 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full façade, then use the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the spires and stone detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 90 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. The cathedral lies to the east of that point.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and line the two towers up with the vertical lines. Hold the phone upright and level so the towers do not lean inwards. If you cannot fit the whole building in, go for a tall portrait-format shot of the façade rather than tilting the phone up. Add a person or a row of passers-by at the bottom to show the scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stone to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not turn white. Use night mode after dark and hold the phone steady against a railing or wall. Avoid panorama here, because moving people can cause odd stitching.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually means softer light and fewer people. After dark, night mode is worth trying.

text.access_note: The cathedral is a working place of worship and a major visitor site, so check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements and any rules about going inside or up the tower.

name: Cologne Central Station
label: Köln Hauptbahnhof
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-16).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/2399559029: the OpenStreetMap point 'Köln Hauptbahnhof'.
notes: Busy station right at the cathedral's feet.

text.description:
Cologne Central Station (Köln Hauptbahnhof) is the city's main railway station and one of the busiest in Germany. About 320,000 travellers pass through on an average day, which makes it the fifth busiest in the country. It sits right next to Cologne Cathedral, so the practical bustle of trains and the cathedral's great stone presence share the same patch of city. That contrast is what makes it a good photo stop.

The first station here opened on 5 December 1859, together with the first bridge over the Rhine beside the cathedral. The building you see today is mostly post-war. Its new hall, with a shell-shaped roof, was inaugurated on 23 September 1957. The railway also links straight to the Hohenzollern Bridge, a bridge with walkways for pedestrians and cyclists on both sides, and the station on the far bank is only about 400 metres away.

For a phone photo, aim for the whole station frontage with people and movement in the foreground, rather than a close-up of a single detail. Stand back, keep the phone level so vertical lines stay straight, and wait a moment for a gap in the crowd or for a good mix of passers-by. Turn gridlines on to help you line things up. If you step inside, be considerate of people hurrying for trains, and keep your phone steady rather than blocking walkways.
text.geographic_location: In the city centre of Cologne, immediately beside Cologne Cathedral, on the left bank of the Rhine. The Hohenzollern Bridge runs from the station across the river towards Köln Messe/Deutz.
text.directions_text: If you are coming from elsewhere in Cologne, use a local journey planner to find a way to the cathedral area. The phone icon on the map is about 100 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the station. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the frontage will not fit in the frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as signs, roof shapes or people at the entrances.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 100 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. From here you look north-east towards the station, with the building filling much of the view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the station up with them so the verticals stay straight. Keep the phone level, since tilting upwards will make the building lean. Include a little foreground, such as people crossing, to give a sense of scale and activity. Take a wide shot first, then a closer one with the telephoto.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the station on the screen to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the building keeps its detail. In the evening, let night mode work and hold the phone steady against your body or a solid surface.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime gives a clear, even view of the whole frontage. Around dusk, lit windows and signs add atmosphere, and night mode can handle the lower light. Quieter hours are easier if you want fewer people in the frame.

text.access_note: The station is a busy public transport building and the outside areas are open to everyone, but rules for photography and use of particular areas can change, so check the official site before you go.

name: Chocolate Museum
label: Chocolate Museum
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Deutzer Hafen' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Deutzer Hafen' (way/23049005): edge nearest the subject (1289 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/334606061: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Chocolate Museum' (64 m across).
notes: Glass-fronted museum on a peninsula in the Rhine.

text.description:
The Chocolate Museum sits on the Rheinauhafen peninsula on the Rhine. Hans Imhoff opened it on 31 October 1993, and the new building was designed with post-modern ship motifs in mind. That is why it looks a little like a glass-and-steel vessel moored at the water's edge. With around 650,000 visitors a year, it is the most visited museum in Cologne.

For a calmer photo than the busy museum frontage, cross to the Deutz side of the river. From here the museum sits in the background across the water, and if you angle yourself well the cathedral can appear in the same picture. The museum's own photo guide suggests this quieter spot for a distant view.

Keep the river in the foreground so the picture feels like a harbour scene rather than a snapshot of one building. Wait for a gap between passing boats or people if you can. If you have time to cross the river, two other angles work well: the Hafendrehbrücke swing bridge, with the harbour water in front of the building, and the Kranhäuser, where the crane houses frame the museum at the end of a corridor.
text.geographic_location: The museum is in Altstadt-Süd, on the Rheinauhafen peninsula in the centre of Cologne, on the left bank of the Rhine.
text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Rheinauhafen area in the south of the old town, or the Deutz bank. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to see the whole scene, then try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the distant museum closer. The ultra-wide (0.5x) will make the building look very small, so keep it for close-up shots.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Deutzer Hafen (right (Deutz) bank of the Rhine, at an angle that includes the museum). The museum in the background across the Rhine, with the cathedral also visible if the angle is right.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the river along the lower third, with the museum on one of the upper intersections. Move a few steps along the bank until the cathedral sits beside the museum without overlapping it. Alternatives are the Hafendrehbrücke swing bridge, or the Kranhäuser for the corridor of crane houses.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the museum to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not turn white. With telephoto, hold the phone steady against your body or a railing, because zoom magnifies shake.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon is a good bet for softer, warmer light on the water, but go when the sky is clear enough to show the cathedral.

text.access_note: The riverside viewpoint is a public outdoor spot, but the museum itself is ticketed, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.

name: Cologne Cathedral Interior
label: Cathedral Interior
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-16).
pin_note: Position from OSM W4532022 (Cologne Cathedral): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: The soaring nave and stained-glass windows inside the cathedral.

text.description:
Step inside Cologne Cathedral and the first thing you notice is the height. The tall, narrow space pulls your eye upward, and the long view down the middle of the building gives a phone photo strong lines and a real sense of scale. Coloured light from the large windows adds to it. This is a place for wide, calm frames, and for small details such as carved stonework, candles and patches of window colour.

The ultra-wide lens (0.5x) suits the main view, because it fits in the height and both side walls. Turn on the gridlines and line them up with the tall columns so the verticals stay straight rather than leaning inwards. The default lens (1x) works well for a more natural view of a single arch or a quiet corner. For details high up, or a close look at a window, try the telephoto/zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) and hold the phone steady against your body.

It is a working place of worship and usually busy, so be patient. Wait for a gap in the crowd, keep your voice low and don't block the aisles. Rules on photography, bags and entry can change, so check the official site before you go.
text.directions_text: Head for the cathedral in the centre of Cologne. From there, follow the signs and the crowd to the entrance and go inside. The phone icon on the map is about 45 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full height and length of the space. Switch to the default lens (1x) for single arches and people, and to telephoto/zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for windows and carved details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 45 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. Take your interior photos once you are inside, looking east along the main space, and stay out of the aisles and any roped-off areas.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Stand centrally and turn on the gridlines. Line up the tall columns with the vertical lines so the building looks straight. Keep the phone level, then tilt it slightly upward only if you want to show more of the vault. For a second picture, move in close to a window or a pillar and use portrait mode or the telephoto for a detail shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap to focus on a mid-tone part of the wall, then lower the exposure slider a little so the bright windows keep their colour. If it is dim, night mode can help, but rest your elbows against your body or a solid ledge and keep still. Turn off the flash.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime, when the windows are brightest, is usually best. Early in the day or late in the afternoon is often quieter, but check the official site for visiting times before you go.

text.access_note: This is a place of worship and a major visitor attraction, so dress respectfully and check the official site before you go for entry, photography rules and any ticketed areas.

name: Museum Ludwig
label: Museum Ludwig
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-16).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/633480736: the OpenStreetMap point 'Museum Ludwig'.
notes: Modern art museum beside the cathedral and the Philharmonie.

text.description:
Museum Ludwig is Cologne's museum of modern art, and the building is as much a subject as the art inside it. It opened in 1986, designed by Peter Busmann and Godfrid Haberer, close to Cologne Cathedral. The Kölner Philharmonie concert hall is in the same building, so you are photographing a big cultural complex rather than a single gallery. Next to it is Heinrich-Böll-Platz, a public square designed by Dani Karavan that sits above the concert hall.

The collection is the reason many visitors come. The museum has around 900 works by Picasso, the third largest Picasso collection in the world after Barcelona and Paris. It also holds well-known Pop Art by Andy Warhol and Roy Lichtenstein, and a large body of early Russian avant-garde work.

Look for the building's overall shape and the way it sits near Cologne Cathedral, and keep a few people in the frame to show its scale. Take a wide shot first, then a closer one of an entrance or a detail of the facade. Check the sign or the official website before you plan to photograph inside, as indoor photography rules can differ from gallery to gallery.
text.geographic_location: On Bischofsgartenstrasse, near Cologne Cathedral. The Philharmonie is in the same building.
text.directions_text: There are no tram or train stops right at this spot, so start from Cologne Cathedral, which is nearby, and head for Bischofsgartenstrasse. The phone icon on the map is about 35 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the building. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you can't fit enough of it in. Use 2x or more for a detail such as a doorway or a window.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 35 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the building's edges parallel to the vertical lines so it doesn't lean. Include a bit of the square or a few passers-by in the foreground to give a sense of size. If you want a second shot, walk a little closer and use the ultra-wide lens for a bolder angle.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the walls keep their detail. Hold the phone with both hands and keep your elbows tucked in.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning is likely to be best, as the sun should be behind you and shining on the side of the building you can see. On a bright day, avoid the midday glare.

text.access_note: The museum is a public cultural building and may be ticketed, so check the official site before you go. Heinrich-Böll-Platz can't be walked on during concerts.

name: Alter Markt
label: Alter Markt
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Alter Markt' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OSM W871395420 (Alter Markt): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Old Town square lined with colourful gabled houses.

text.description:
Alter Markt is a square in Cologne, and it makes a classic postcard picture. The view that most people photograph is from beside the Jan von Werth fountain, looking south. The 61-metre City Hall tower rises over a row of colourful gabled houses, with the fountain in the foreground. The mix of bright facades, the tall tower and the statue gives you plenty to work with, even in a single frame.

The fountain makes a good anchor for the shot. Put it on the right of the picture and let the tower sit above the rooftops in the middle. The stepped gable of the Gaffel Haus is a good second subject on the same square. Its painted plaster looks best when low sun falls on it.

The square is busiest at two times of year. The Christmas market is the most photographed season, so if you want the tree lights in the picture, frame the tree carefully, and expect crowds to make a clean, empty shot hard to get. When Carnival opens at 11:11, large crowds gather around the fountain. At those times, hold your phone a little higher, or accept people in the frame as part of the atmosphere. At quieter times you can take your time and try both a wide view and a closer one of the tower.
text.geographic_location: Alter Markt is in Cologne, with the 61-metre City Hall tower rising over the houses when seen from the fountain. The Fischmarkt and its colourful houses are right next door.
text.directions_text: No nearby station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from central Cologne and head for Alter Markt. By taxi or hired scooter, ask for Alter Markt. Once you are there, look for the City Hall tower and the Jan von Werth fountain, which is where the phone icon on the map is. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the classic view of the houses, tower and fountain. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the crowd or the Christmas stalls make it hard to fit everything in. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the tower over the rooftops.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Face south toward the Rathaus. From here the 61-metre tower rises over the colourful gabled houses, with the fountain in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and place the fountain on the right, with the tower near the centre line. Keep your phone level so the houses don't lean. For a different angle on the same square, try the stepped gable of the Gaffel Haus, which looks good when low sun lights its painted plaster.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the tower to set focus and exposure, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky looks washed out. In the Christmas market season, tap on the tree and lower the exposure slightly so the lights show up clearly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day is usually calmer if you want a cleaner view of the fountain and houses. Low sun is kind to the Gaffel Haus gable. In the Christmas market season, go in the evening for the lights, but expect crowds.

text.access_note: Alter Markt is an open public square, but for events such as the Christmas market or Carnival, check the official site before you go.

name: Great St. Martin Church
label: Great St. Martin
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Fischmarkt' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Fischmarkt' (relation/7859023): middle (79 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/25270980: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Groß Sankt Martin' (68 m across).
notes: Romanesque church with a tall tower, the centrepiece of the Old Town skyline.

text.description: Great St. Martin is a Romanesque church whose tall crossing tower is a landmark of Cologne's Old Town. The best-known view is from Fischmarkt, the cobbled square in front of it. From there the tower and the church's eastern end rise above a row of pastel gabled houses, which gives you colour, old stone and a clear subject in one frame. The church stands where an island in the Rhine once lay. Its foundations, from around 960 AD, rest on the remains of a Roman chapel. The buildings you see today were put up between 1150 and 1250, and the eastern end has an unusual clover-leaf plan of three apses. It was badly damaged in the Second World War and restoration finished in 1985. A storm in 1434 brought down three of the four tower gables, and one struck a nearby fish market. As of 2009, the church is used by a branch of the Monastic Fraternities of Jerusalem. For a phone photo, stand on Fischmarkt with the Rhine behind you and face the church. Include some of the gabled houses and the cobbles so the tower has context. If you want a different view, the Rheinboulevard across the river lines up the church tower, the Cathedral and the Old Town houses along the waterfront.
text.geographic_location: In Cologne's Old Town (Altstadt), a short distance from the Rhine bank. The Fischmarkt square lies right in front of the church.
text.directions_text: No tram or Underground stop is listed for this spot, so start from the Old Town beside the Rhine and head for the Fischmarkt square. By taxi or hired scooter, ask for Fischmarkt in the Old Town. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x), which shows the tower, the church's eastern end and the gabled houses together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the square is crowded or you want more of the houses. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the tower top.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Fischmarkt (Old Town side, facing the church's west front and tower). The church tower and west front rising above the pastel gabled houses and the cobbled fish-market square, with the Rhine behind the photographer.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the tower on one of the vertical lines, with the gabled houses filling the lower part of the frame. Try to keep your phone level so the tower does not lean. Guides also recommend the Rheinboulevard across the river, which shows the church tower, the Cathedral and the gabled houses along the waterfront.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not wash out and the stonework keeps its detail. Take a few shots, since people crossing the square will come and go.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon gives warm light on the tower, according to one guide. Another suggests early morning for the eastern light. Either way, check the light on the day.

text.access_note: The square is an open public space, but the church has reduced opening hours and is a place of worship, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Keeping the phone level helps stop the tower leaning in the photo (a general phone-photography tip).
People crossing the square may walk through the frame, especially at busy times.
The ultra-wide lens (0.5x) can help fit more of the houses in when the square is crowded.
Visitors to a working church are usually expected to dress modestly and keep quiet.

name: Hohenzollern Bridge
label: Hohenzollern Bridge
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-16).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/616123417: the OpenStreetMap point 'Hohenzollernbrücke'.
notes: Rail bridge covered in love locks, with the cathedral behind it.

text.description: The Hohenzollern Bridge carries trains across the Rhine in Cologne, with a footpath alongside the tracks. It was built between 1907 and 1911 and opened by Kaiser Wilhelm II on 22 May 1911. Its iron truss arches make a strong, repeating pattern, and that is what makes it work so well in a phone photo. The lines of the arches lead the eye along the bridge, and a train passing through adds some life to the picture. More than 1,200 trains use it every day, so you rarely wait long. The bridge is 409 metres long. It was blown up in 1945, and the rebuilt version was finished in 1959. Equestrian statues of Prussian kings and emperors stand beside the ramps on both banks. The railings are also famous for love padlocks, which were estimated at around 500,000 in June 2015. The phone icon on the map is about 230 m west of the subject. From there you may be able to fit much of the bridge into the frame with the ultra-wide lens, without any special kit. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) lens for as much of the span as possible and the default lens (1x) for a tidier crop. Switch to zoom if you want to pick out the arches and trains. Keep to the pedestrian walkway and stay clear of the tracks.
text.geographic_location: The bridge crosses the Rhine in the centre of Cologne and links Köln Hauptbahnhof on the west bank with Köln Messe/Deutz on the east bank. It sits on the central axis of the cathedral.
text.directions_text: From there the bridge lies to the east. The phone icon on the map is about 230 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for as much of the span of arches as you can fit in, then try the default lens (1x) for a cleaner view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the arches and any train crossing.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 230 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the line of the arches along the lower third, with sky filling the rest. Wait for a train to enter the arches, then take a few shots or a Live Photo so you can choose the best moment. If you zoom in, the repeating arches stack up neatly.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bridge to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour and the ironwork stays dark and clear. Hold the phone steady with both hands.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or the hour before sunset usually gives softer light on the ironwork. After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows on a wall or railing to keep it steady.

text.access_note: The walkway is a public pedestrian route alongside the railway, but check the official site before you go in case of works or closures.
claims_not_in_sources: From the stand-here point you may be able to fit much of the bridge into an ultra-wide (0.5x) frame.
Early morning or the hour before sunset usually gives softer light.
The walkway is a public route open to pedestrians, though works or closures can happen.
Trains are frequent enough that you rarely wait long for one to cross.

name: Romano-Germanic Museum
label: Romano-Germanic Mus.
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Roncalliplatz' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Roncalliplatz' (way/89615664): middle (80 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/965473: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Romano-Germanic Museum' (84 m across).
notes: Roman Cologne museum beside the cathedral, built around the Dionysus mosaic.

text.description:
The Romano-Germanic Museum is Cologne's archaeological museum, built around the remains of a Roman town villa. It opened in 1974 on the site of a 3rd-century villa that was found in 1941. The Dionysus mosaic, from around A.D. 220/230, still lies where the Romans laid it. The museum also holds what is described as the world's largest collection of Roman glass vessels.

For a phone photo, the appeal is the setting rather than the museum alone. The building is low and modern, and Cologne Cathedral rises directly behind it. That is the classic view of the museum, and it shows how the Roman site sits right beside the cathedral.

The main building has been closed for a full renovation since 2018, so the front may be partly hidden by works. The collection is shown for now at the Belgian House on Cäcilienstraße 46, a different building that is not part of this photo spot. Take the picture as a view of the square, the museum and the cathedral together. Keep the phone upright if you want the full height of the cathedral, or turn it sideways to include the width of the frontage. If the front is screened, use the cathedral as your main subject and let the museum sit low in the foreground.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Cologne, on Roncalliplatz directly south of Cologne Cathedral. The museum stands right beside the cathedral.
text.directions_text: Start from Cologne Cathedral, which is right next to it, and walk to Roncalliplatz on its south side. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the low museum frontage and the cathedral together. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural view. Try telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the cathedral towers behind the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Roncalliplatz (in front of the museum's facade, with the cathedral behind). The low museum building in the foreground with Cologne Cathedral rising behind it, the classic framing of the museum.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the low museum building across the bottom of the picture and let the cathedral fill the space above it. Turn on gridlines and keep the horizon level, so the cathedral does not lean. Hold the phone upright for the cathedral's height, or sideways for the frontage. If scaffolding or hoardings cover the front, make the cathedral your main subject and use the museum as a foreground band.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the cathedral to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the stonework keeps its detail. Use panorama only if you stand still and move the phone slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft light earlier or later in the day suits the cathedral stonework better than harsh midday sun.

text.access_note: Roncalliplatz is the square in front of the museum. The museum building is closed for renovation, so check the official site for current visiting arrangements at the Belgian House.

photo.from: Own photo, taken 61 m from the phone icon

name: Cologne City Hall
label: Cologne City Hall
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Rathausplatz' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Rathausplatz' (way/493219568): middle (41 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/16186002: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Historisches Rathaus' (108 m across).
notes: Historic town hall with its Renaissance loggia and Gothic tower.

text.description:
Cologne City Hall is the city's town hall and Germany's oldest, with a documented history of some 900 years. What you see today is a patchwork built over centuries: a 14th-century hall building, a Gothic council tower finished in the 1410s, and a Renaissance loggia (an open arcaded porch with a balcony above) built between 1569 and 1573. The tower rises 61 metres and is covered in stone figures, so it rewards a slow look. The loggia was once used for public speeches. Much of the complex was destroyed in the war and rebuilt, but the front portion and part of the tower survived. The tower's bells also play a carillon four times a day.

It photographs well because the Gothic tower and the Renaissance loggia sit side by side, so one frame can show several centuries of building. Rathausplatz, the open square in front, is the classic place for a wide shot of the whole complex. It is also where people gather to watch the tower's clock figure before the hour. The Spanischer Bau, a Renaissance-style building from the early 1600s (rebuilt in 1953), stands on the north-western side of the square and can add depth to a wider frame.

Take your wide shot first, then move closer for details such as the loggia arches and the carved figures. Look at the screen before you shoot: a tall tower makes it easy to tilt the phone upwards, and the building will then lean in the picture.
text.geographic_location: In Cologne's Innenstadt (city centre), just off Hohe Straße. It sits between the two squares of Rathausplatz and Alter Markt.
text.directions_text: Make your way to the Innenstadt and look for Rathausplatz, the square at the front of the City Hall, just off Hohe Straße. No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so check a local journey planner for the best way to get there from elsewhere in Cologne. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the tower, loggia and square into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the tower's stone figures and the clock.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Rathausplatz. Wide view of the Gothic council tower and the Renaissance loggia together, framing the whole historic complex.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line. Keep the phone level and hold it upright so the tower does not lean. Include a little of the square in the foreground to give a sense of scale. For a different view, try Alter Markt for the older rear face of the building, or Deutzer Brücke for a distant view across the Rhine. Conditions at Alter Markt may have changed, so check on site.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the stonework to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky is washing out. Use telephoto for the carved figures rather than walking into other people's pictures.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and there are fewer people. If you want the clock figure, arrive a few minutes before the hour.

text.access_note: Rathausplatz is an open public square, but the space between the historic building and the Spanischer Bau is closed on wedding days, so check the official site before you go, especially if you want to reach the main entrance.
claims_not_in_sources: Holding the phone tilted upwards at a tall tower makes the vertical lines lean inwards, and gridlines help keep it level.
Lowering the exposure slider can stop a bright sky washing out in the photo.
Using telephoto for details avoids having to step into other people's shots.

name: 4711 House
label: 4711 House
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Glockengasse' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/4544839246: the OpenStreetMap point 'House of 4711'.
notes: Home of the original Eau de Cologne with its carillon.

text.description: The 4711 House is the original shop of the famous Eau de Cologne brand, at Glockengasse 4 in the middle of Cologne. The scent has been made in the city since at least 1799, and the shop is a popular stop for visitors. The name comes from the number given to a house on this street when the French numbered Cologne's buildings in 1794. That house was later pulled down, but the number stuck to the brand. For a photo, the draw is the neo-Gothic street front, with its carillon (Glockenspiel) and the brand's lettering. The street is narrow, so getting the whole façade in one frame takes a little effort. Stand on the opposite side of the street, switch to the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) and keep your phone level so the building doesn't lean. The 4711 name is easy to read, which makes the picture instantly recognisable. If you want something tighter, the corner where the building meets Schwertergasse gives an angled view, and the zoom lens picks out the carillon. The façade is said to look especially good when it is lit up at Christmas. The house is also a shop and museum, so decide whether you want a quick street photo or a visit inside, and check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The 4711 House stands on Glockengasse in central Cologne, near the corner with Schwertergasse. It is on a narrow street among the shops and buildings of the city centre.
text.directions_text: Start from the centre of Cologne and head for Glockengasse; the house is at number 4. By taxi or hired scooter, use the street address, Glockengasse 4. You will see the neo-Gothic front and the carillon once you are on the street. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit as much of the façade as the narrow street allows. Use the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched view, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the carillon.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. The house itself is the subject.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line the vertical edges of the building up with them so it doesn't lean. If the whole façade won't fit, frame the carillon and lettering together. For an alternative, try the corner by Schwertergasse for an angled view, or zoom in on the carillon from the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the façade to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky behind it is bright. If you shoot when the façade is lit up, try night mode and hold the phone steady against your body or a wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Guides mention the façade looks especially good when lit up at Christmas. At other times, daylight shows the stonework and lettering clearly.

text.access_note: The front of the building can be photographed from the public street, but the house is a shop and museum, so check the official site before you go and before taking photos inside.

name: Basilica of St. Ursula
label: St. Ursula
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Ursulaplatz' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Ursulaplatz' (way/22887905): point nearest the subject (190 m long).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/27780576: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'St. Ursula' (71 m across).
notes: Romanesque basilica with the Golden Chamber of relics.

text.description: The Basilica of St. Ursula is one of the twelve Romanesque churches of Cologne, and it stands on its own open square. That setting is what makes it easy to photograph on a phone: you can stand back far enough to get the west front and the bell tower in one frame, with the trees around the square softening the edges. The nave and main tower are Romanesque, while the choir was rebuilt in the Gothic style, so the building mixes two periods. The church was designated a Minor Basilica on 25 June 1920. It sits on the site of an ancient Roman cemetery, and the legend of St. Ursula and her 11,000 virgins is tied to the place. Inside, the Golden Chamber has walls covered in bones arranged in patterns and letters. These remains were found in 1106 in a mass grave. Then move in on details such as the tower, the doorway and the stonework. A second option is the side of the square lined by historic houses, which gives a more framed, less open picture of the church. Keep your phone upright so the tower does not lean, and check the official site before you go if you want to see or photograph inside.
text.directions_text: There are no stations or tram stops listed close to this spot, so start from central Cologne and come by taxi or hired scooter, asking for Ursulaplatz. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole west front and tower. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the tower will not fit or you want more of the trees and square in the frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the tower and stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Ursulaplatz (in the middle of the square, facing the church front and tower). The west front and bell tower of the Romanesque basilica, framed by the open square and the trees around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line a vertical grid line up with the tower, so the building stands straight. Leave some of the square and trees at the edges of the frame to give a sense of place. For a different feel, try the side of the square lined by historic houses, where the houses frame the church more closely.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the church front to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. If you use ultra-wide, stay square-on to the front to limit stretching at the edges.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daylight when the front is lit gives the clearest view of the stonework. Afternoon to early evening is likely to give warmer light on the west front. Go early if you want fewer people on the square.

text.access_note: The square and the outside of the church are open to see, but the Golden Chamber and any photography inside may have their own rules, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The west front is likely to catch warmer light in the afternoon and early evening.
Early in the day the square is likely to have fewer visitors.
Bright sky can make stonework look darker, so lowering exposure helps.

name: Rheinauhafen Crane Houses
label: Kranhäuser
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Severinsbrücke' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Severinsbrücke' (way/375981247): edge nearest the subject (1146 m across); moved 30 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/37766848: large area 'Rheinauhafen' (1810 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Modern crane-shaped buildings in the old harbour on the Rhine.

text.description:
The Rheinauhafen is a former commercial harbour on the Rhine, just south of Cologne's old town. It was developed in the 1880s and has been rebuilt as a district of offices, cultural venues, hotels and homes, with a marina in the old harbour basin. Its best-known buildings are the three Kranhaus blocks. From south to north they are KranhausPLUS, Kranhaus1 and Pandion Vista, and their shapes echo the harbour cranes that once stood here. Construction on the regeneration project started in 2002, and the middle building, Kranhaus1, won an international award in 2009.

The three buildings are strong, simple shapes, and they photograph well against the river and sky. The best phone view is from the footpath on Severinsbrücke, looking south. You are close enough to make the buildings look big, yet far enough back to fit all three in one frame. The bridge's steel arch and the Rhine add a frame and some depth. Trams and traffic can make the bridge vibrate, so plant your feet, tuck your elbows in and take a few frames rather than just one. If you have more time, Poller Wiesen on the far bank shows the crane houses with the cathedral behind them, and Harry-Blum-Platz gives a closer view from the harbour side.
text.geographic_location: In Cologne, on the Rhine just south of the old town. The Rheinauhafen runs along the river between the Severinsbrücke and the Südbrücke.
text.directions_text: Head for the Severinsbrücke. Go onto the footpath of the bridge and stop where you can look south along the harbour. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to fit all three crane houses in one frame. Try ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the bridge's steel arch around them. Use 2x-3x zoom, if your phone has it, for a tighter shot of the buildings' angled shapes.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Severinsbrücke (footpath on the bridge, looking south toward the Rheinauhafen). All three L-shaped Kranhäuser close in front of the lens, with the Rhine and the bridge's steel arch framing them.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up a vertical grid line with the edge of one of the buildings so they don't lean. Let the bridge's steel arch fill one side of the frame and the river the bottom. For a different view, the far bank at Poller Wiesen shows the crane houses with the cathedral behind them, but it is busy in summer.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the buildings to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the sky keeps its colour. Hold the phone with both hands and brace your elbows against your body, because trams and traffic can make the bridge shake. In dim light, use night mode only when you are standing steady and wait for the shaking to stop.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Blue hour, just after sunset, when the colour contrast at dusk suits the bridge view. Allow for passing trams and traffic shaking the bridge.

text.access_note: The bridge footpath and the harbour promenade are open public spaces, but I haven't checked for current closures or works, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Trams and road traffic use Severinsbrücke and can make the footpath vibrate.
Poller Wiesen is busy in summer.
Looking south from the bridge, the sun may be in front of you around midday, so the buildings can look darker.
The bridge footpath and harbour promenade are public, open-air spaces.

name: St. Gereon's Basilica
label: St. Gereon
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Kopf des Heiligen Gereon' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Kopf des Heiligen Gereon' (node/3615363521): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/38246033: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'St. Gereon's Basilica' (88 m across).
notes: Late Roman decagonal church with a striking dome.

text.description:
St. Gereon's Basilica is a Roman Catholic church in Cologne with a long, layered history, which is a good part of why it photographs so well. The oldest part is an oval Roman building from the second half of the 4th century, and a church here is first mentioned in 612. The east end, with its two square towers and rounded apse, was added in the 12th century. In the 13th century the old oval core was encased and topped with a decagonal dome. That dome is the largest built in the West between Hagia Sophia and the cathedral in Florence. The church became a minor basilica in 1920.

As a foreground option, look for the large sculpted head of St. Gereon in front of the church, on the park side. It gives a more distinctive alternative to the standard church view, with the towers and apse rising behind it. Check on the day exactly where it stands. Walking along Gereonskloster you can also frame the tower and the building's overall bulk from the street. If the park is open and in good order, its small green setting makes a pleasant frame for the east end. Three sides of the church are hard to see without crossing the street, so you may need to step back or cross to fit it in.
text.geographic_location: St. Gereon's Basilica stands just north-west of the ancient Roman city centre of Cologne, on a slight rise next to the street Gereonskloster and the small park Gereonsdriesch.
text.directions_text: There are no stations or tram stops listed close by, so head for the street Gereonskloster, by taxi or hired scooter if you are coming from further away. If you are already walking along Gereonskloster, look for the sculpted head in front of the church. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the church, or for the head and church together if you find the sculpture. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the towers are being cut off, or to telephoto (2x or more) for a tighter view of the towers and apse.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (in front of the church, on the park side near Gereonskloster). The large sculpted head of St. Gereon in the foreground, with the basilica's towers and apse behind it. From here you can frame the basilica's towers and apse.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: If you find the head, put it in the lower part of the frame and let the towers and apse rise behind it. Turn on the gridlines and line up the church with one of the vertical lines to keep the walls straight. For a different view, try Park Gereonsdriesch, which shows the east end with the apse and two towers framed by the park. You can also walk along Gereonskloster for the tower and the overall mass of the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the church or the head to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not turn white. Hold the phone level to keep the towers upright, and take a few frames at different distances.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft, even light suits the stonework, so a bright, softly overcast day is a good choice.

text.access_note: The outside, the sculpture and the park can be seen from the street, but opening arrangements for the church interior are not given here, so check the official site before you go; photography inside is generally allowed without flash.

name: Rhine Promenade Deutz
label: Deutz Rhine Skyline
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Rheinboulevard' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Rheinboulevard' (way/360111604): middle (501 m across).
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-17: was the Deutz district centre; moved onto the OSM Rheinboulevard (W360111604)).
notes: Classic skyline view of the cathedral and Old Town across the Rhine.

text.description:
The Rhine Promenade in Deutz runs along the east bank of the river, and its best-known photo spot is the Rheinboulevard, with an upper terrace and wide concrete steps that face west across the water. From here the Cologne Cathedral and the Hohenzollern Bridge sit together in one frame, with the Rhine filling the foreground. That is why it is such a popular place for a classic Cathedral-and-bridge picture from the Deutz side.

The steps work as a ready-made viewing platform. You can sit, pick your height and take your time. Guides often mention sunset as a favourite moment here, and some suggest going early in the morning when it is quiet. The terrace gives you a slightly higher view, and the steps let you drop lower so the river takes up more of the picture.

On a phone, keep it simple. Use the default lens (1x) to get the Cathedral and the bridge side by side, and switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more river and sky. Turn on the gridlines so the water stays level. If you fancy a different angle, the Deutzer Brücke gives a skyline view with the river and promenade below, and Rheinpark offers a wider sweep across open water. Exact positions vary slightly, so check on the day: have a look along the terrace and steps and pick the spot where the Cathedral and the bridge line up best for you.
text.geographic_location: On the east (Deutz) bank of the Rhine, with a view west across the river to Cologne Cathedral and the Hohenzollern Bridge. The promenade and its Rheinboulevard terrace and steps face west towards the Cathedral and the Hohenzollern Bridge.
text.directions_text: Head for Deutz, on the east bank of the Rhine opposite the Cathedral, and walk to the riverside. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the Cathedral and the bridge together. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for more river and sky, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the Cathedral on its own.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Rheinboulevard (east (Deutz) bank, upper terrace and concrete steps facing west toward the Dom). The Cologne Cathedral and the Hohenzollern Bridge framed together across the Rhine, with the river in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and keep the horizon level, with the river along the bottom third. Place the Cathedral and the bridge so neither is cut off. Sit low on the steps if you want more water in the foreground. For a different view, try the Deutzer Brücke for the skyline with the promenade below, or Rheinpark for a wider sweep of the skyline.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the Cathedral to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour. After sunset, use night mode and rest your phone on something steady so it does not shake.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Golden hour into blue hour (sunset and just after). Early morning is another option if you want it quieter.

text.access_note: This is an open public terrace and set of steps by the river; no charge is noted, but check the official site before you go for any closures.

name: Cologne Tower
label: Colonius Tower
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'MediaPark' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Mediapark' (way/770591291): edge nearest the subject (661 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/23113718: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Kölnturm' (52 m across).
notes: Telecommunications tower west of the centre.

text.description:
The Cologne Tower (KölnTurm) is a 44-storey glass office skyscraper in the Köln-Neustadt-Nord district, near the MediaPark. It stands 148.5 m high, or 165.48 m with its antenna. It was built between June 1999 and November 2001 and is the second-tallest building in the city, after the Cathedral. Kohl & Kohl designed it with the Paris architect Jean Nouvel. Many media companies work here, which fits the MediaPark setting.

It photographs well because of its glass facade. Pictures of the Cathedral and the Old Town skyline are screen-printed onto the glass, and which of them show depends on the light. The calmer, cleaner shot is from the MediaPark lakeside. There the tower can be reflected in the artificial lake or framed above it, with a bridge and other modern buildings alongside. Stand and look east across the water.

For a second, more dramatic picture, walk to the foot of the tower and tilt your phone up to catch the full height of the glass. The lake is the easier option for a tidy, balanced photo. Both are quick to do, so try each and keep the one you prefer.
text.geographic_location: The tower is in the Köln-Neustadt-Nord district of Cologne, beside the MediaPark and its artificial lake.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. Head for the MediaPark area in Neustadt-Nord and go to the lakeside stand-here point on the map. From there the tower is to the east, about 1 minute on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) from the lakeside to get the tower and its reflection. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you walk to the base and want the full height from below. Telephoto (2x or more) can isolate the upper glass facade if you want a tighter shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in MediaPark (lakeside, looking across the artificial lake toward the tower (bridge over the lake area)). The tower reflected in or framed above the MediaPark lake, with a bridge and other modern buildings in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the water's edge on a lower line. Keep the tower upright and let its reflection fill the lower part of the picture. Include the bridge or nearby buildings to give a sense of scale. As an alternative, from the tower's own base, tilt the phone up with the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) to catch the full height of the glass.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the glass keeps its detail and the sky doesn't wash out. Wait for ripples to settle before you press the shutter.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the water is still, so the reflection is clearer. The facade pictures change with the light, so it is worth checking the tower at different times of day if you have time.

text.access_note: The lakeside is in a public park and the tower is an office building, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.

name: KölnTriangle Viewing Platform
label: KölnTriangle Deck
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/21113435: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Köln Triangle' (44 m across).
notes: Rooftop viewing deck with a panorama of the cathedral and city.

text.description:
KölnTriangle is a 103-metre high-rise in Deutz, directly across the Rhine from Cologne Cathedral. The architect Dörte Gatermann designed it, and it was completed in 2006. Next to the tower is a much larger six-storey office block. The top floor and roof hold a public observation deck with views over the whole city.

From the deck you can photograph the Cathedral together with the Rhine and the city around it. From the deck the Cathedral's twin spires stand out clearly against the skyline. The river gives you a line that leads the eye towards it.

The phone icon on the map is on the building itself, so you take your photos from the deck. Start with a wide view of the whole skyline. Then move closer on the Cathedral and look for details such as the spires and the river. Walk the full length of the deck, because each side gives a different angle. Wipe your phone lens before you start, and keep the phone close to any glass or railing to cut down on reflections. Access to observation decks can change, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In Deutz, directly across the Rhine from Cologne Cathedral.
text.directions_text: Use a map app to navigate to the KölnTriangle in Deutz, the district directly across the Rhine from the Cathedral. The building is a tall, easily seen tower there, and the observation deck is at the top. The phone icon on the map is on the building itself, so there is no further walk once you are inside. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole skyline and the default lens (1x) for most shots. Switch to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the Cathedral's spires.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Shoot from the observation deck at the top, looking across the Rhine towards the Cathedral.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the river along the lower third, with the Cathedral just off-centre. Take one wide shot of the whole view, then a telephoto shot of the Cathedral alone. Keep the phone close to the glass or railing, and keep your hand steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the Cathedral to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not wash out. Try panorama mode for a sweep along the river, and move slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon or early evening usually gives softer light and a warmer sky. After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows on a ledge to keep the phone still.

text.access_note: The observation deck is publicly accessible, but access arrangements may change, so check the official site before you go.
